video_title: The Fed Is Facing An Impossible Problem | Judy Shelton & Thomas Hoenig
gist: Judy Shelton and former Kansas City Fed president Tom Hoenig argue the new Worsh Fed is boxed in: $2 trillion of annual federal borrowing forces it to either monetize (via QE and the FIMA repo facility now backstopping Japan) or let long rates rise sharply, with no third option absent Congressional fiscal repair. They attack the post-2008 ample-reserves/IORB framework as a broken transmission mechanism that pays banks (40%+ foreign-owned) not to lend, want a return to scarce reserves and market-set long rates, see gold displacing the dollar as the top reserve asset and a gold anchor as eventually unavoidable, and both endorse a 0% inflation target over 2%.

themes.theme: Worsh's opening agenda and Fed internal politics

insights.claim: Kevin Worsh's stated framework is to let market supply and demand set the cost of capital rather than have rates imposed by the FOMC committee, which Judy Shelton reads as a genuine free-market reorientation of Fed policy.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: If the Fed steps back from pegging the curve, term premia and long-end volatility should rise structurally; position for a steeper, more market-determined yield curve.
insights.quote: we should let free market forces of demand and supply determine the cost of capital rather than having rates imposed by a committee

insights.claim: Worsh is hawkish on returning inflation to 2% but is deliberately not committing to interest on reserve balances as the only tightening tool, keeping optionality on using the balance sheet instead.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Markets pricing Fed tightening only through the policy rate may misjudge risk; balance-sheet-led tightening would hit duration and MBS spreads rather than the front end.
insights.quote: he's not committing to the idea that the only way you do that is by raising the interest on reserve balances interest rate

insights.claim: Hoenig says Worsh knows the right policy but faces circumstances that make it very difficult to execute, and that a painful conflict between shrinking the balance sheet, raising rates and hitting 2% inflation is unavoidable at some point.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Expect a policy shock later rather than sooner; the market's current calm about Fed intentions has an expiry date.
insights.quote: Uh the conflict is unavoidable at some point.

insights.claim: Shelton believes the Fed has become too prominent, too powerful and too political, and that sitting members are now using friendly journalists at major newspapers as personal Fed whisperers to express skepticism about Worsh's initiatives.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Expect more Fed-source leaks and contradictory signals in the press; headline-driven rate volatility around FOMC communication is likely to increase.
insights.quote: I've always thought the Fed was was too prominent, too powerful, and too political.

insights.claim: Hoenig reads Christopher Waller's public remarks as a deliberate challenge to the new chair, breaking the Fed's traditional culture of debating internally then supporting the chair publicly.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Dissent risk at the FOMC raises the odds of surprise vote splits and of policy drifting from the chair's stated path.
insights.quote: there is a reaction to Kevin kind of a a we're challenge you reaction to Kevin

insights.claim: Shelton objects that Waller voted yes with the majority while airing sentiments from what was meant to be a private pre-meeting dinner, which she reads as undercutting the incoming chair's authority rather than honest dissent.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Signals a governance fight inside the Fed that could complicate Worsh's ability to deliver framework reform on schedule.
insights.quote: there's nothing wrong uh with disagreeing and Chris did not vote no.

insights.claim: Hoenig frames the core US problem as the debt itself, which pressures the Fed to monetize it because the alternative is visibly higher yields.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Every Fed decision should be read as a choice between higher long yields now and more inflation later; own inflation-protected or hard assets against either branch.
insights.quote: putting a lot of pressure on the Fed to monetize that debt. uh otherwise you're going to see yields go up

insights.claim: US national debt is growing at roughly $2 trillion a year, about half a trillion every quarter that must be placed with buyers, according to Hoenig.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Auction sizes of ~$500bn per quarter are the dominant supply variable for the long end; watch tail sizes and dealer takedowns as the stress gauge.
insights.quote: our national debt continues to grow at $2 trillion a year

insights.claim: Hoenig's binary: if the Fed refuses to absorb the debt it pushes rates higher sooner, and if it agrees it continues indirectly funding the national debt, so there is no clean exit from the current setup.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: The trade is symmetric-risk on nominal bonds: either a rate shock or a currency/inflation debasement; gold and real assets hedge both.
insights.quote: it will be uh pushing rates higher sooner. Uh and if it says yes, it will be continuing uh in in one sense indirectly to fund uh our national debt.

insights.claim: Hoenig lays out three exits from the debt trap: keep monetizing with a balance sheet growing faster than potential GDP, stop cold in a Volcker-style shock, or have Congress slow deficit growth so the economy grows out of the debt.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: A clean three-branch decision tree for scenario-weighting rates, dollar and gold exposure over the next several years.
insights.quote: we'll monetize the debt because there's no other choice

insights.claim: Between December 2025 and April 2026 the Fed was buying roughly $40 billion a month, which Hoenig characterizes as being back in QE.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence the Fed is already the marginal buyer; any stated intent to stop is a de facto tightening the market has not priced.
insights.quote: between December of last year and April, the Fed, you know, $40 billion a month. They were back in QE

insights.claim: Hoenig says the second option, the Fed refusing to grow its balance sheet beyond potential growth, means interest rates go up a lot and amounts to another Volcker moment.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Tail risk of a disorderly rate repricing if the Fed genuinely stops accommodating; duration is the most exposed asset class.
insights.quote: we're not going to do that anymore. That means interest rates are going to go up a lot and it means that this is a vulker moment we're talking about here

insights.claim: Hoenig cites two precedents where the US grew out of its debt, post-World War II and the Clinton-Gingrich mid-1990s, both associated with roughly 4% real growth and high real productivity.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Sets the benchmark for a benign resolution: without a sustained ~4% real growth regime, debt math forces monetization.
insights.quote: our average growth rate was closer to 4%. Real productivity was high and we grew out of it

insights.claim: Hoenig argues the Fed must abandon Powell's practice of staying silent on fiscal policy and explicitly tell Congress it will not monetize the debt, while offering a transition period.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Any Worsh testimony that names fiscal policy directly would be a regime-shift signal for the long end and the dollar.
insights.quote: has to say we cannot monetize your debt

insights.claim: Shelton criticizes Powell for repeatedly telling Congress the fiscal path is unsustainable over the long run while never saying that the long run has already begun.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Illustrates why Fed warnings have zero market or political impact; only an action, not testimony, changes fiscal behavior.
insights.quote: I want to be on the record that the fiscal situation is is unsustainable and over the long run

insights.claim: Shelton argues the only genuine way out is productive economic growth, because if Congress keeps overspending the Fed must either accommodate the issuance or impose restrictive rates that punish the private sector while the government keeps paying high rates at auction anyway.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Implies rate hikes are a private-sector tax that shifts capital and power to government; favors sectors less dependent on external credit.
insights.quote: it starts shifting more power to the federal government at the expense of the private sector and that is not healthy

insights.claim: Hoenig says Worsh's position is not materially different from Volcker's, with inflation out of control plus a worse deficit problem, and that any Fed attempt at discipline would be attacked viciously by all parties as Volcker was.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Political-tolerance limits, not economics, are the binding constraint on Fed tightening; expect policy to fold before inflation is fully beaten.
insights.quote: the Fed will be attacked viciously if they were to do that um as as it was when Vulker did it

insights.claim: As foreign buyers pull back, Hoenig says the Fed becomes the only remaining enabler of continued deficit spending, so the entire fiscal burden lands on the central bank's balance sheet decision.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: The marginal-buyer question is the single most important variable for long rates; track foreign official holdings alongside Fed SOMA.
insights.quote: This time we have even a more out of control uh spending or deficit problem.

insights.claim: Hoenig says the debt problem cannot be solved quickly and must be worked out carefully over the next five to six years, implying a multi-year regime of elevated rates and constrained policy rather than a single crisis event.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Sets a 5-6 year horizon for the debt workout; favors staying short duration and long real assets across that window.
insights.quote: it has to be carefully solved over the next five to six years

themes.theme: Japan, the FIMA repo backstop and the yen line

insights.claim: The Fed's 2020-vintage FIMA repo facility, which Shelton says carries a $60 billion limit, is the mechanism through which Japan is now being encouraged by Treasury Secretary Bessant to obtain dollars without selling Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Watch FIMA repo usage in the Fed's weekly H.4.1 as a real-time gauge of foreign official dollar stress and hidden support for the Treasury market.
insights.quote: the FEMA facility and that stands for uh foreign and international monetary authorities repo facility and there is a a 60 billion limit on that

insights.claim: Hoenig characterizes the arrangement bluntly as the Treasury looking to the Fed to fund Japan's purchases of US debt so Japan does not have to sell Treasuries and depress prices, and says he is very concerned about it.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Frames swap/repo lines as backdoor monetization; a former FOMC voter publicly calling it that raises the political risk around the facility.
insights.quote: the Treasury is looking to the Fed to really fund Japan's purchases of US debt

insights.claim: Japan is the largest foreign holder of US Treasuries with close to $1.2 trillion, making its forced selling to defend the yen a first-order driver of US yields.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Japanese FX intervention and Treasury holdings are now a direct input to US long-rate forecasting.
insights.quote: Japan is the largest holder. They have close to 1.2 trillion.

insights.claim: Shelton says the pandemic overturned the assumption that crises drive a flight into Treasuries, because foreign countries instead dumped Treasuries to obtain actual dollars, which is precisely why the collateralized repo facility was created.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Undermines the standard safe-haven trade: in acute stress, Treasuries can be sold, not bought, by foreign officials.
insights.quote: these foreign countries were were dumping treasuries because they really wanted the dollar the actual dollars

insights.claim: Shelton says Bessant deliberately left a cabinet-meeting to-do list visible to reporters noting buying another 5 to 10 billion of Japanese yen, signalling to speculators that the US will not let the yen-dollar rate move much beyond 160.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: An effective official line near 160 USD/JPY caps the carry trade's upside and makes short-yen positioning asymmetrically risky.
insights.quote: literally said to-do list by another 5 to 10 billion of of Japanese yen

insights.claim: Japan's debt at roughly 200% of GDP is twice the US's ~100%, and its suppressed rates are what make it vulnerable to the massive carry trade that Shelton says threatens international financial stability.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Any BOJ normalization forcibly unwinds the carry trade; treat Japanese rate moves as a global risk-asset trigger.
insights.quote: as bad as ours is, about 100% debt to GDP, Japan's is twice as bad. 200% of GDP and outstanding debt

insights.claim: Hoenig identifies a direct trap: letting Japanese rates rise would appreciate the yen but simultaneously make it harder for the US to fund its own debt, so both sides of the Japan problem hurt the Treasury market.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: There is no benign Japan scenario for US long rates; both yen appreciation and Japanese selling raise US funding costs.
insights.quote: um how many dollars do you want eventually and how much of this do you feel obligated to take?

insights.claim: Shelton relays Trump's argument that the US, as the dominant reserve currency and the world's best credit risk, sits midway in the pack on policy rates and consistently above the ECB and Bank of Japan, which she treats as evidence the international monetary system is a nonsystem where money is made on anomalies.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Signals continued White House pressure for lower US policy rates regardless of inflation, a dollar-negative political overhang.
insights.quote: why is it that we're midway in the pack in terms of of what our um target um interest rate is from our central bank?

insights.claim: Despite Japan's much higher debt ratio, Shelton judges the US to be in the worse position because its debt is widely held by foreigners, citing the post-Liberation-Day tariff episode when US debt was rejected as a protest move.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Foreign ownership converts US fiscal policy into a geopolitical vulnerability; trade tension now transmits directly into the Treasury market.
insights.quote: after Liberation Day and tariffs were introduced, just kind of a rejection of US debt as a protest move

insights.claim: Hoenig believes Worsh wants the long end of the yield curve to move up on its own without Fed interference, treating higher market-set long rates as the intended outcome rather than a policy failure.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Do not expect the Worsh Fed to cap or twist down long yields; steepeners are aligned with the chair's apparent intent.
insights.quote: And Kevin sees that and I think that's why he wants the loan side of the yield curve to move up without him interfering.

insights.claim: Shelton says gold has recently displaced the US dollar as the number one reserve asset held by major central banks, and cites Jacques de Larosiere's view that gold overtaking the euro was a terrible sign for the euro as the analogue for what it now means for the dollar.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Central bank gold accumulation is a structural, price-insensitive bid; treat it as a floor under gold and a signal on dollar reserve status.

insights.claim: Hoenig, a former Kansas City Fed president, says all fiat systems have historically fallen apart and that the world is slowly being forced by necessity toward greater reliance on a gold standard for international stability, against its own will and nature.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: A mainstream former FOMC voter endorsing eventual gold anchoring is itself a signal about elite opinion drift; supports strategic gold allocation.
insights.quote: being forced if you will to rely more on a gold standard uh going forward just for the international uh stability of it

insights.claim: Shelton recounts Alan Greenspan saying after 18 years as chair that without some governor on issuance, whether a gold standard or a currency board, there will be a tendency to overissue money and credit not calibrated to the economy's needs, producing deleterious inflation.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Frames inflation as a structural feature of unconstrained fiat rather than a cyclical event, arguing for permanent inflation hedges.
insights.quote: experience has shown that unless there is some kind of governor on the issuance

insights.claim: Shelton argues fiscal discipline may require a balanced budget amendment driven by a state governor-led movement involving figures like DeSantis or Greg Abbott, rather than any self-restraint by Congress.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Places the probability of near-term Congressional fiscal repair very low, which by Hoenig's framework leaves monetization as the default path.
insights.quote: it might take a very strong governor-led initiative to deliver a balanced budget amendment

insights.claim: Shelton's case for gold rests on automatic discipline: under an international gold standard, individuals in the real economy who judged conditions too frothy could convert dollars to gold, which mechanically contracted the money supply without any committee decision.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Explains why she frames market-set rates as a partial substitute for gold discipline, and why she supports Worsh letting markets, not the Fed, set the cost of capital.
insights.quote: the beauty of of the international gold standard was the um automatic discipline

insights.claim: Shelton's gold-backed Treasury Trust bond proposal was not launched on July 4th as many expected but remains a live idea she has pitched at the highest levels, having been displaced on that date by the Trump accounts initiative.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: A gold-convertible Treasury issue remains a live policy tail-risk that would reprice both gold and the long end if announced.
insights.quote: I have presented it. I have given my most intense elevator speech at at the highest levels.

insights.claim: Shelton wants the US to be first to adopt a gold anchor with a convertibility rate controlled by people in the real economy, framing it as the route to a level international monetary playing field rather than a return to a fixed-price gold standard by decree.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Defines the specific policy shape to watch for: convertible Treasury instruments, not a formal peg.
insights.quote: I have no objection to using gold as an anchor. But I want the US to be the first to utilize that anchor

insights.claim: Shelton argues equity markets are the ultimate way for workers to own the means of production, citing SpaceX making millionaires of its employees, and frames broad equity ownership as the free-market answer to rising sympathy for socialism.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Policy tailwind for retail equity ownership vehicles and employee-ownership structures as an explicit political project.
insights.quote: really the ultimate way for the workers to own the means of production. see companies like like SpaceX making millionaires out of their employees

insights.claim: Shelton says US gold reserves are the largest in the world at 261 million ounces, she is confident they exist, and a walk-through of Fort Knox by the president would be a public relations bonanza.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: A publicized audit or revaluation of the 261m-ounce hoard is a live catalyst for gold and for dollar-confidence narratives.
insights.quote: I'm shocked that people don't trust the government.

insights.claim: Shelton wants a forensic audit that also establishes there are no encumbrances on US gold, noting the Bank for International Settlements engages in gold-linked transactions and other countries store gold at the New York Fed.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Encumbrance, not physical existence, is the real question for gold-collateralized instruments; a clean audit is a precondition for gold-backed bonds.
insights.quote: the bank for international settlements makes some sometimes some some gold linked transactions

insights.claim: Hoenig is confident the gold is physically there because any steady leakage would already have shown up as market volatility, but still supports an audit as low-cost reassurance.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Deflates the missing-gold thesis while keeping the audit as a cheap confidence catalyst rather than a solvency question.
insights.quote: So there's no reason why not to do it or to walk through the vault and then have the audit.

insights.claim: Shelton wants any gold backing US bonds legally ring-fenced as collateral that no future administration can sell, held solely to honor bondholder conversion.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Defines the credibility test for any gold-linked Treasury issue: statutory non-sale of the collateral.
insights.quote: collateral that can never be sold off by a future administration

themes.theme: Broken transmission: IORB, ample reserves and MBS

insights.claim: Since 2008 the Fed has relied on interest on reserve balances rather than the small-portfolio open-market operations of the Volcker era, so what is still called the federal funds rate is a fundamentally different mechanism, and a Worsh task force is examining that transmission channel.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: A framework review of IORB is the most underpriced Fed policy risk of 2026; it would change how every rate decision transmits to credit.
insights.quote: So they may still call it a federal funds rate, but it's nothing like the system we had under Paul Vulker

insights.claim: Shelton argues a 25bp hike translates operationally into paying commercial banks more on riskless reserves sitting at the Fed so they make fewer loans, which chokes small and medium-sized businesses precisely when the remedy for inflation should be increasing supply, not killing demand.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Implies the Worsh Fed may fight inflation without hiking IORB; small-cap and regional bank lending conditions are the tell.
insights.quote: We are going to pay commercial banks who are required to keep cash reserves sitting at the Fed doing nothing.

insights.claim: Shelton says over 40% of the interest the Fed pays on reserve balances goes to foreign-owned banks, a fact she believes would provoke public anger if better known.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Politically combustible statistic that raises the odds of legislative or Fed-led changes to IORB, a direct hit to bank net interest income.
insights.quote: over 40% of the interest paid by the Fed on reserve balances is going to foreignowned banks

insights.claim: Reserves and excess reserves were almost nothing prior to 2019 and now stand at roughly three trillion dollars, which the panel uses to question why the ample-reserves regime is needed at all.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: A shift back toward scarce reserves implies draining trillions in reserves, a major liquidity headwind for risk assets.
insights.quote: if you look at the chart on on reserves and excess reserves, it was very low. It was almost nothing prior to 2019

insights.claim: Shelton says the ample-reserves system destroyed price discovery in the so-called fed funds rate and that Worsh would like to return to a scarce-reserve system where the Fed manages at the margin as a smaller, not dominant, player, though it cannot be done overnight.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: The single most consequential structural change on the table; a scarce-reserve transition means sustained balance-sheet runoff and higher money-market volatility.
insights.quote: so that you do uh say manage at the margin and the Fed's a smaller player, not the dominant player

insights.claim: Hoenig calls the Fed's purchase of mortgage-backed securities credit allocation in another form, says entering that market in the first place was inexplicable and inexcusable, and expects the Fed to unwind slowly for fear of disrupting an already stressed housing market.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: MBS runoff will stay slow, keeping mortgage spreads artificially supported; do not expect active Fed MBS sales.
insights.quote: the fact that they went down this path in the first place was really inexplicable and and inexcusable

insights.claim: Shelton says the Fed carries roughly $800 billion in capital losses on its Treasuries and MBS, and because of its accounting it prefers runoff to sales, but 20- and 30-year mortgage securities barely run off so they will linger on the balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Explains why balance-sheet normalization will take a decade or more, capping how hawkish the Fed can actually get via the balance sheet.
insights.quote: capital losses on on their treasuries and MBS but um when you you're not going to have much of a runoff on on 20 and 30year securities

themes.theme: Shocks beyond the Fed's reach: oil and AI credit demand

insights.claim: Hoenig distinguishes a one-shot price-level change from ongoing energy inflation caused by reduced production capacity, saying only the latter is genuinely harmful, and that the Fed cannot solve either the energy problem or the productivity problem.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: The right question for policy is whether the oil shock is a level shift or a capacity loss; only capacity destruction forces the Fed to slow the economy.
insights.quote: But if it's all if it's ongoing continuing because we're reducing production capacity that's going to be harmful to the economy.

insights.claim: Hoenig says the only real fix for an oil-driven inflation shock is ending the war and stabilizing energy prices, not Fed rate hikes, which can only adjust money creation around the shock.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Geopolitical de-escalation, not FOMC action, is the tradeable catalyst for the inflation path; watch the Gulf rather than the dot plot.
insights.quote: the Fed cannot solve the energy problem. That's external.

insights.claim: Shelton attributes part of the rise in long yields to competition for long-term capital, with investors preferring AI companies and innovation over riskless government paper, meaning the government is competing against profitable but risky investments for the same pool.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: AI capex funding is a structural upward force on the term premium; corporate credit supply competes directly with Treasury issuance.
insights.quote: there's competition for that long-term capital and people would rather invest it with these these AI companies

insights.claim: As hyperscalers tap credit markets more heavily, bond investors gain more choices and the Treasury loses its captive bid, a crowding-out dynamic the host and both guests agree is entirely outside the Fed's control.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart, host
insights.so_what: Monitor AI-related investment-grade issuance volumes as a leading indicator of Treasury auction stress and term-premium widening.

themes.theme: Asset inflation, the inequality backlash, and a 0% target

insights.claim: Shelton concedes the Fed has clearly exacerbated the wealth and income gap because holders of financial assets did far better than those without, while noting roughly half the population does hold a 401k.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: A sitting-adjacent policy adviser conceding Fed responsibility for inequality raises the political price of future asset-price support.
insights.quote: the Fed clearly has exacerbated the the wealth and income gap

insights.claim: Shelton's judgment is that unequal monetary outcomes are not bad monetary policy but bad social policy, and the real danger is when people come to believe monetary favoritism is working against them and that the whole system is rigged.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Frames political risk to the Fed's independence as a function of perceived fairness, not measured inflation.
insights.quote: That's when you have people saying the whole system's rigged

insights.claim: Hoenig argues that celebrating sub-2% CPI from 2010 to 2018 was a mistake because asset values were being doubled at the same time, and that inflation arbitrarily creates winners and losers regardless of merit.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Argues for judging monetary policy on asset prices as well as CPI, which implies today's policy is far looser than headline inflation suggests.
insights.quote: everyone said from 2010 to 2018 uh you know the consumer price index was below 2% and that was bad

insights.claim: Hoenig warns that anyone who studies socialism knows it makes everyone poorer, that America has lost that lesson, and that the wealth loss to the very people such policies aim to help would be far greater than the current gap.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: Political-regime risk is now a macro variable; a socialist policy turn would be the tail scenario for US equity and credit valuations.
insights.quote: socialism knows it's the way to make everyone poorer

insights.claim: Hoenig has argued for decades that the correct inflation target is 0%, not 2%, because mild deflation is no worse than mild inflation and averaging zero over the cycle would do the world a big favor.
insights.speaker: Tom Hoenig
insights.so_what: A serious constituency for a 0% target exists among Worsh-aligned thinkers; a lower target would mean structurally higher real rates.
insights.quote: if you're between those two and you manage accordingly and you come up on average at zero, you've done the world a big favor

insights.claim: Shelton fully endorses a 0% inflation target and mild deflation, arguing falling prices are the natural order as technology raises living standards at lower cost.
insights.speaker: Judy Shelton
insights.so_what: Two credible Fed-adjacent voices converging on 0% raises the odds the 2% target itself is contested in the coming framework review.
insights.quote: I couldn't agree more with Tom's final statement, by the way, about getting down to zero inflation and mild deflation
